candidates.attacker_control: Any authenticated (or otherwise READ-granted) user controls the request path/parameters: GET /computer/<name>/systemProperties, /computer/<name>/env (getEnvironment/getEnvVars), /computer/<name>/threadDump, and the node system-info page /computer/<name>/systemInfo, which in-tree is documented (core/src/main/resources/hudson/node_monitors/TemporarySpaceMonitor/help.html) and rendered by the jenkins.slaves.systemInfo.* extensions (SystemPropertySlaveInfo, EnvVarsSlaveInfo, ThreadDumpSlaveInfo).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The node 'System Information' side panel label exists (core/src/main/resources/hudson/slaves/SlaveComputer/sidepanel2.properties, systemInfo_*.properties), so the page may have been intended for users who can see a node - if so, the ungated getters are by-design rather than a vuln. The renderer views (.jelly) and all tests are absent from this snapshot, so I could not verify whether a view-side permission condition existed or whether Stapler serves these getters directly. I verified that analogous sensitive accessors are gated (getLogText/CONNECT, doConfigDotXml/EXTENDED_READ, doDumpExportTable/ADMINISTER, HeapDump download/RUN_SCRIPTS) and that Jenkins.getAllThreadDumps() is ADMINISTER-gated, which is counterevidence that the omission is deliberate. I could not confirm that a permission check was later added upstream (no network/ground-truth allowed), and I did not find a security-advisory marker for these methods in the snapshot.
candidates.impact: Information disclosure from the Jenkins controller and agents to any user with Overall/Read: environment variables and JVM system properties frequently contain credentials/proxy settings/paths (e.g. tokens passed via env, java.class.path, temp dirs), and thread dumps reveal internal state, class loaders and code paths that aid further attacks. Depending on deployment these are secrets that Jenkins normally restricts to administrators/ExtendedRead users. This is a read-only disclosure (no write/RCE directly), but it breaks the trust boundary between read-only users and node-level operational data.
candidates.prerequisites: Overall/Read permission (default for all authenticated users; also anonymous if READ is granted) and a running Computer (master or an agent). No POST, token, CSRF crumb or admin permission is required for a GET; the only coarse gate is Jenkins.getTarget() which checks only Overall/Read.
candidates.root_cause: hudson.model.Computer is not a StaplerProxy and defines no getTarget(), and ComputerSet.getDynamic() returns any Computer without a permission check; the public getters Computer#getSystemProperties(), Computer#getEnvironment(), Computer#getThreadDump() and Computer#getHeapDump() likewise perform no checkPermission()/hasPermission() before returning sensitive data to the requesting JVM. Nearby sensitive methods are gated (getLogText() requires CONNECT, doConfigDotXml() GET requires EXTENDED_READ, doDumpExportTable() requires ADMINISTER, HeapDump.doHeapDump() requires RUN_SCRIPTS), so the omission on these getters is inconsistent with the surrounding authorization model.
candidates.title: Missing permission checks on Computer information getters expose node JVM system properties, environment variables and thread dumps to users with Overall/Read
candidates.trace: Request /computer/(built-in)/systemInfo (or the individual getter URLs) -> Jenkins.getTarget() passes because the caller has READ (jenkins/model/Jenkins.java:4595-4606) -> Jenkins.getComputer() getter binding exposes ComputerSet (Jenkins.java:1444-1447) -> ComputerSet.getDynamic() calls Jenkins.getComputer(token) with no permission check (ComputerSet.java:200-202) -> Computer instance exposes public getters with no permission check: getSystemProperties()/getEnvironment()/getThreadDump() (Computer.java:1157-1187, 1219-1226) execute on the master/local channel (getChannel()) and return the JVM system properties, environment variables and thread dump; getHeapDump() (1231-1233) also returns an object whose download is only gated later in HeapDump.doHeapDump.
candidates.unverified: Runtime reachability was not verified: this snapshot has no .jelly files (all removed by the source filter), so I cannot see whether /computer/<name>/systemInfo or the getter URLs route/render as expected, nor whether a view-level permission gate exists. Whether Stapler getter/view routing exposes these methods with only Overall/Read is inferred from Jenkins conventions (e.g. /me -> Jenkins.getMe(), /api -> Jenkins.getApi, /computer -> Jenkins.getComputer) and from in-tree references (help.html, SlaveSystemInfo contract), not from execution. Whether upstream considered this a vulnerability (and the exact fix: ADMINISTER vs Computer.EXTENDED_READ, or removing the page for non-admins) is unconfirmed.

coverage_summary: Scope reported by get_source_scope: 9,725 readable files, no excluded symlinks/sensitive paths/oversize files; binary-like files are skipped by the reader. The snapshot contains only main-source-like files: no test directories and no .jelly views (verified via path globs), so only Java/resources/JS/properties/build files were reviewable. I enumerated the tree top-down, then audited core/cli/war Java in the security-sensitive areas: DirectoryBrowserSupport, VirtualFile, FilePath, FileParameterValue, ParametersAction, User/UserIdMapper/UserIdMigrator, ApiTokenProperty/BasicApiTokenHelper/BasicHeader*Authenticator, RedactSecretJsonInErrorMessageSanitizer, ClassFilterImpl/CustomClassFilter, XStream2/SafeURLConverter/XStreamDOM, ACL/SidACL/SparseACL/Permission checks, CrumbFilter/DefaultCrumbIssuer/CrumbExclusion, Jenkins and Jenkins.CLIAction endpoints, Computer/ComputerSet/SlaveComputer/RemotingDiagnostics, AbstractItem/Run/Job/AbstractProject/View/ItemGroupMixIn/ListView, CLI commands, Plugin/AssetManager/Descriptor/doResources/RSS, UpdateCenter/UpdateSite/DownloadService signatures, JSONSignatureValidator and Secret/SecretRewriter. Many known hardening fixes are present; the Computer information getters and /secretKey getter stood out as ungated, with Computer getters selected as the strongest candidate. I did not inspect every file of the 9,725 (large classes such as Queue.java, Jenkins.java internals, update-center and JenkinsRule-like machinery were only spot-checked), and the CLI client module, war JS assets and i18n resources were only sampled.
limitations: No runtime verification: code was not compiled, built or executed; no HTTP requests were issued, so reachability of the cited URLs is inferred, not confirmed.

Tests and all .jelly views were removed by the snapshot filter, so view-level permission checks and the exact rendering path of /computer/<name>/systemInfo could not be inspected; a fix in a removed view would not be visible.

Exact release/commit identity is uncertain: poms say 2.107.4-SNAPSHOT but the tree contains APIs annotated @since 2.129 (e.g. User#getUserFolder) and references to '2.129+' backports, so I could not pin the advisory/fix this snapshot precedes.
No precomputed source-relation index (B0 condition) and no ground-truth/CVE/patched-version data were available, so identification of the 'intended' single vulnerability is inferential.

Several large, high-traffic classes (Queue.java, full Jenkins.java, UpdateCenter.java, PluginManager.java, security realm implementations) were only partially reviewed; other vulnerabilities may exist outside the inspected paths.
The candidate itself is a lead: I could not confirm whether the node system-info access is by design or whether an upstream fix added ADMINISTER/EXTENDED_READ checks to these getters.

rejected_leads.lead: jenkins.model.Jenkins#getSecretKey()/getSecretKeyAsAES128() are public, unannotated getters returning the master secret key, and Jenkins.getTarget() only requires Overall/Read, so GET /secretKey may disclose the key to any read user (Jenkins.java:1341-1364).
rejected_leads.reason: Source evidence is clear, but the key is explicitly documented as deprecated because 'Due to the past security advisory, this value should not be used any more to protect sensitive information' (the marker file is even named secret.key.not-so-secret), so exposure may be accepted/by-design and impact is limited to legacy-format Secret values and pre-SECURITY-49 API tokens; no fix marker or reachability evidence could be confirmed in the snapshot. Mentioned only as an uncertain lead.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson.FilePath#unzip(File,File) and #readFromTar() extract archive entries without any canonical/descendant validation (FilePath.java:603-637 and 2359-2391), allowing Zip/Tar Slip path traversal when an untrusted archive is extracted.
rejected_leads.reason: Objective missing check, but no core HTTP entry point feeds attacker-controlled archives to these methods (core caller is FileSystemProvisioner for build-owner archives; installIfNecessaryFrom pulls from admin-configured URLs). Exploitation depends on plugins/build steps using these APIs with attacker-supplied archives, so attacker control is speculative; likely long-standing upstream behavior rather than the injected/known fix.

rejected_leads.lead: hudson/model/RSS.java forwardToRss() builds the Jelly view path from the request parameter 'flavor' after only replacing '/' with '_' (RSS.java:82-86), and Jenkins.doResources()/doHelp() do classloader resource lookups from user paths.
rejected_leads.reason: Descriptor.doHelp has a '..' check (Descriptor.java:917-921), doResources is restricted to an extension allow-list and relies on classloader resource resolution, and no attacker-controllable .jelly/resource exists in core; no concrete traversal/read primitive could be demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Reverted-fix hypotheses for DirectoryBrowserSupport symlink escape (SECURITY-904), FileParameterValue folder traversal (SECURITY-1074), SafeURLConverter URL deserialization (SECURITY-637), $redact secret redaction, XStream/JEP-200 ClassFilter, CSRF crumb filter, CLI command permission checks, AbstractItem config.xml secret masking, ItemGroupMixIn copy-with-secrets, Run.doArtifact ARTIFACTS check, _doScript POST check, Plugin.doDynamic path checks and AssetManager '..' check.
rejected_leads.reason: All of these hardening checks were verified present in the snapshot and therefore rejected as the target issue.

summary: Jenkins core snapshot (poms report 2.107.4-SNAPSHOT; content includes 2.129-era APIs such as User#getUserFolder, BasicApiTokenHelper and the SECURITY-904/1074/637 hardening artifacts). I audited the HTTP-reachable security surface: DirectoryBrowserSupport/VirtualFile/FilePath, FileParameterValue, XStream2/SafeURLConverter, User/UserIdMapper, ApiTokenProperty/BasicHeader authenticators, ClassFilterImpl, ACL/SidACL, Csrf filter/CrumbIssuer, Jenkins endpoints, Computer/ComputerSet, ItemGroupMixIn/AbstractItem/Run/Job/View, CLI commands, RemotingDiagnostics, Plugin/AssetManager/Descriptor/doResources and RSS. Most known 2017–mid-2018 hardening is present. The single strongest issue I can support from source is that Computer's sensitive information getters (JVM system properties, environment variables, thread dump) have no permission check while equivalent sensitive accessors are gated, and the Computer object itself has no getTarget/StaplerProxy gate. I cannot runtime-confirm reachability (the .jelly views are filtered out of this snapshot), so this is submitted as a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
